titulo: Remote work and productivity: what the evidence says

fuente.nota: Written for the language panel. The figures are approximate and should not be cited as a source.

parrafos: Are people who work from home more productive, or are they quietly doing the laundry between video calls? Few questions in the world of work have generated so much heat and so little light. Six years after the pandemic forced millions of office workers to set up desks in their kitchens, the research has finally caught up with the debate, and its conclusions are more nuanced than either side would like.

First, some perspective. Before 2020, working from home was a marginal arrangement in most European countries, concentrated in a few professions and among senior staff. During the lockdowns, almost everyone who could work remotely did so. Since then, the share of days worked from home has fallen back, but it has settled at a level several times higher than before the pandemic. The most common model today is not fully remote work but a hybrid arrangement, in which employees spend two or three days a week in the office and the rest at home.

The early evidence looked encouraging. A well-known experiment carried out at a large Chinese travel company in the early 2010s found that call-centre staff who were randomly assigned to work from home became noticeably more productive. They took fewer breaks, lost less time commuting and were less often off sick. Many managers drew the conclusion that offices were an expensive habit, and some technology firms announced that their employees could work from anywhere, for ever.

Later studies have painted a more complicated picture. Research on fully remote workers in other settings, such as data entry or customer service, has sometimes found lower productivity, particularly among less experienced staff. The reasons seem to be a mix of distractions at home, weaker supervision and, above all, the loss of informal learning. Junior employees who sit next to experienced colleagues pick up skills simply by listening and asking questions. On a video call, that kind of spontaneous mentoring tends to disappear.

Hybrid work appears to strike a better balance. A follow-up experiment at the same Chinese company, involving graduate employees in roles such as engineering, marketing and finance, found that working from home two days a week had no measurable effect on performance or promotions. It did, however, reduce resignations substantially, especially among women and employees with long commutes. Since replacing a worker is costly, lower staff turnover can translate into significant savings for employers.

Measuring productivity is itself part of the problem. For a call-centre worker, output can be counted in calls answered or sales closed. For a lawyer, a designer or a policy analyst, it is much harder to define. Surveys show that employees tend to believe they are more productive at home, while managers are more likely to think the opposite. Both may be partly right: workers often count the time saved on commuting, which does not appear in the company's figures, while managers notice the loss of collaboration, which is difficult to quantify.

At the level of the whole economy, the picture is even harder to read. Aggregate productivity statistics are affected by many factors at once, from energy prices to investment and changes in the mix of industries. So far, there is no clear evidence that the shift to remote work has either boosted or damaged productivity across the economy as a whole. Some economists argue that the main gains may come indirectly, by allowing firms to recruit from a wider pool of talent and keeping in work people who would otherwise have left the labour market.

That last point deserves attention. Remote and hybrid work have made it easier for parents of young children, people with disabilities and those living far from big cities to hold down good jobs. In countries with low employment rates among women, or with regions suffering from depopulation, this could have important social and economic effects. Some rural areas in Spain and elsewhere have actively tried to attract remote workers with fast internet connections and affordable housing, although the results have so far been modest.

There are also costs that do not appear in company accounts. City centres that depended on office workers have seen footfall in shops and restaurants fall, and commercial property values have come under pressure in many cities. Some workers report feelings of isolation and a blurring of the line between working hours and private life. In response, several European countries, including Spain, have adopted laws that regulate remote work and recognise a right to disconnect outside working hours.

Meanwhile, the pendulum has started to swing back in some sectors. A number of large banks and technology companies have ordered employees to return to the office for most of the week, citing the need to strengthen company culture and innovation. Critics suspect that, in some cases, these mandates are also a discreet way of reducing staff numbers, since some employees prefer to resign rather than give up their flexibility. Others point out that firms in a competitive labour market risk losing talent to rivals that offer more freedom.

So what does the evidence say? In short, remote work is neither a miracle nor a disaster. Its effects depend on the type of task, the experience of the employee and, crucially, on how well it is organised. Fully remote work can suit some independent, well-defined jobs, but carries risks for training and teamwork. Hybrid arrangements, if they are planned carefully, seem to offer most of the benefits with few of the costs. The real challenge for managers is no longer deciding where people work, but learning how to manage them well wherever they are.
titulo_es: Remote work and productivity: what the evidence says
resumen_es: Analysis of what studies reveal about the effect of remote and hybrid work on productivity, and of its social, urban and labour consequences.

ideas_clave.idea: Since the pandemic, working from home has stabilised well above its previous level, mostly in hybrid form, and research now offers more balanced conclusions about its effect on productivity.
Early experiments suggested home-based workers were more productive, but later studies of fully remote work found losses, especially for junior staff who miss out on informal learning.
Hybrid work two days a week did not harm performance and cut resignations, which saves employers money.
Productivity is hard to measure in many jobs, workers and managers perceive it differently, and no clear economy-wide effect has been observed so far.
Remote work can broaden access to jobs for parents, disabled people and rural residents.
It also has drawbacks, such as emptier city centres, isolation and blurred working hours, which some countries address through regulation.
Some large firms are now ordering staff back to the office, a move that may hide other aims and risks driving talent away.
Overall, the impact of remote work depends on the task, the worker and the organisation; well-planned hybrid models appear to work best and good management is the key.

resumen_modelo: The article reviews the research on whether working from home makes employees more or less productive. After the pandemic, remote work declined from its peak but stabilised far above pre-2020 levels, mainly in a hybrid form. Although an early experiment in a Chinese call centre showed productivity gains thanks to fewer breaks, no commuting and less sick leave, later research on fully remote jobs has sometimes found the opposite, largely because inexperienced staff lose the informal learning that comes from working alongside colleagues. By contrast, hybrid arrangements appear not to affect performance while sharply reducing resignations, which lowers costs for firms. Nevertheless, productivity is difficult to measure in many occupations, and employees and managers tend to disagree about it; moreover, no clear effect can yet be detected in national statistics. Beyond productivity, remote work may help parents, disabled people and rural residents to access good jobs, but it has also hurt city-centre businesses and created risks of isolation, which has led countries such as Spain to legislate, including a right to disconnect. Some companies are now demanding a return to the office, which may cost them talent. The author concludes that remote work is neither a miracle nor a disaster: its success depends on the type of job and above all on good management.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Working from home has now returned to the level it had before the pandemic.
preguntas.cita: it has settled at a level several times higher than before the pandemic
preguntas.explicacion: Remote work has fallen since the lockdowns, but it has stabilised at a level several times higher than before the pandemic.

preguntas.enunciado: Choose the correct option according to the text.
preguntas.pregunta: What is the most common way of working today, according to the article?
opciones: A hybrid arrangement with two or three office days
respuestas: A hybrid arrangement with two or three office days
preguntas.cita: The most common model today is not fully remote work but a hybrid arrangement
preguntas.explicacion: The text says the most common model is hybrid, with two or three days in the office. It explicitly rules out fully remote work and does not mention coworking spaces.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 3 that means “travelling to work every day”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning “travelling to and from work”.
preguntas.explicacion: “To commute” is to make the daily journey between home and work; “commuting” is the -ing form that appears in the text.

preguntas.enunciado: Choose the correct option according to the text.
preguntas.pregunta: According to later studies, what is the main reason why fully remote work can reduce productivity?
opciones: The loss of informal learning from colleagues
respuestas: The loss of informal learning from colleagues
preguntas.cita: above all, the loss of informal learning
preguntas.explicacion: The text highlights “above all” the loss of informal learning, especially for less experienced employees. Connections, energy and longer working days are not mentioned as a cause.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: In the follow-up experiment, hybrid workers were promoted less often than office workers.
preguntas.cita: had no measurable effect on performance or promotions
preguntas.explicacion: The experiment found no measurable effect on either performance or promotions.

preguntas.enunciado: Find an expression in paragraph 5 that means “the rate at which employees leave and are replaced” (es: rotación de personal).
preguntas.pregunta: Find an expression meaning “the rate at which employees leave and are replaced”.
preguntas.cita: lower staff turnover can translate into significant savings for employers
preguntas.explicacion: “Staff turnover” is the rate at which staff leave and are replaced. Watch out: “turnover” on its own, in British accounting, also means a company's total sales (es: volumen de negocio).

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: Why do employees and managers often disagree about productivity at home?
respuestas: Workers tend to include the time they save by not commuting, which does not show up in company data, while managers see the loss of collaboration, which is hard to measure. So each side focuses on a different part of the picture.
preguntas.cita: workers often count the time saved on commuting, which does not appear in the company's figures
preguntas.explicacion: Both are partly right because they measure different things: the time saved by the worker versus the lost collaboration perceived by the manager.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: There is clear evidence that remote work has increased productivity across the whole economy.
preguntas.cita: there is no clear evidence that the shift to remote work has either boosted or damaged productivity
preguntas.explicacion: The text says there is no clear evidence of an aggregate effect, either positive or negative.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Spanish rural areas have received European funds to attract remote workers.
preguntas.explicacion: The text says that some rural areas have tried to attract remote workers with good connections and affordable housing, but it does not mention any European funding.

preguntas.explicacion: The text mentions the fall in customer numbers in city-centre shops and restaurants. It does not talk about taxes, accidents or lower wages.

preguntas.cita: these mandates are also a discreet way of reducing staff numbers
preguntas.explicacion: “Mandates” are compulsory orders or instructions; here, the orders to return to the office.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: Why do some critics think return-to-office orders may have a hidden purpose?
respuestas: Because some employees would rather resign than lose their flexibility, so ordering them back to the office can be a quiet way for companies to cut staff without formal layoffs.
preguntas.cita: since some employees prefer to resign rather than give up their flexibility
preguntas.explicacion: It is an inference question: the order to return leads to voluntary resignations, which amounts to cutting staff without layoffs.

Fully remote work is the best option for all employees
The effects depend on the task, the worker and the organisation
Productivity is always higher in the office
respuestas: The effects depend on the task, the worker and the organisation

preguntas.explicacion: The author concludes that remote work is neither a miracle nor a disaster and that its effects depend on several factors. The other options are extreme positions that the text rejects.

tribunal.pista_es: Comprehension: the boom during the pandemic, the partial retreat and the consolidation of the hybrid model.

Experience of the worker and informal learning
